20	\title{AgentPProf: Semantic Profiling for AI Agent Traces}
21	
22	\begin{abstract}
23	% Beat 1: Context
24	AI agents produce complex execution traces spanning prompts, LLM calls,
25	tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects. As deployments grow
26	to hundreds of sessions, both human operators and automated analysis
27	pipelines need aggregate views---not just per-execution debugging.
28	
29	% Beat 2: Problem
30	Existing observability tools organize events into fixed session/span
31	hierarchies suited for single-run debugging but unable to fold events
32	across sessions by semantic work category. CPU flame graphs solve the
33	equivalent aggregation problem for programs, but they rely on
34	deterministic function names; agent prompts are natural language and
35	cannot be folded directly.
36	
37	% Beat 3: This paper
38	We show that agent profiling reduces to two abstractions once intent
39	recognition restores the deterministic-label precondition. An
40	\emph{operation} is a uniform weighted record for any agent activity; an
41	\emph{operation stack} is a field projection chosen at query time.
42	Sessions and spans become optional fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
43	\toolname implements this model with pluggable intent-recognition
44	backends (regex rules, local LLM tagging, unsupervised clustering) and
45	produces flame graphs, pprof profiles, and structured JSON consumable by
46	both developers and analysis agents.
47	
48	% Beat 4: Results
49	On 325 real agent sessions, semantic labels separate 90\% of
50	system-effect weight that flat views merge. On four public datasets
51	(34{,}539 operations), operation-stack profiling reduces inspection work
52	by 90\% versus flat summaries and fragmentation by 45\% versus
53	fixed-session drilldown. Leave-dataset-out mapping achieves V-measure
54	above 0.7 on 7/9 held-out datasets.
55	\end{abstract}

59	%% ===================================================================
60	\section{Introduction}
61	
62	AI agent systems produce execution traces that interleave prompts, LLM
63	calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, process events, and benchmark
64	labels. As agent deployments scale to hundreds of sessions and tens of
65	thousands of calls, both developers and automated analysis agents need
66	to answer aggregate questions: which categories of work consume the most
67	tokens, where do repeated failures concentrate, and how does cost
68	distribute across semantic task families? Existing observability
69	tools---LangSmith~\cite{langsmith}, Langfuse~\cite{langfuse},
70	Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, OpenTelemetry GenAI~\cite{otel}---organize
71	events into per-execution timelines and span trees, enabling
72	single-run debugging. But no existing tool provides an aggregate view
73	that folds heterogeneous events across sessions into a cost or frequency
74	distribution grouped by semantic work category.
75	
76	CPU profilers solved the equivalent problem for programs: flame
77	graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} fold millions of function-call samples into
78	a single chart where width represents cost. The key enabler is
79	\emph{deterministic} function names that merge identical call stacks.
80	Agent traces break this assumption---prompts are natural language, and
81	two prompts expressing the same intent share no characters. We develop
82	this gap and the design requirements it implies in
83	\S\ref{sec:background}.
84	
85	The central insight is that agent observability requires
86	\emph{profiling}---aggregate, semantic, cross-session cost
87	attribution---not only per-execution debugging, and that the obstacle to
88	applying classical profiler techniques is the nondeterminism of
89	natural-language identifiers. This paper presents \toolname, a profiler
90	that restores aggregate flame-graph analysis for agent traces. The
91	profiler is built on two abstractions: an \emph{operation} (a uniform
92	weighted record for any agent activity) and an \emph{operation stack}
93	(a field projection chosen at query time). Sessions, spans, and trace
94	identifiers are operation fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
95	\emph{Intent recognition}---mapping free-form prompts to stable labels
96	through pluggable backends (regex rules, local LLM tagging, or
97	unsupervised clustering)---restores the deterministic-label precondition
98	that flame-graph folding requires.
99	
100	Some existing tools take steps toward semantic grouping: Datadog LLM
101	Observability clusters user messages by topic, and Laminar extracts
102	structured signals from traces. These characterize \emph{input
103	distributions} (``30\% of users ask code questions'') but not
104	\emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks consume 40\% of the
105	token budget''). \toolname produces the latter through folded-stack
106	aggregation where width represents cost.
107	
108	This paper makes three contributions:
109	
110	\begin{enumerate}
111	\item \textbf{Insight: agent profiling reduces to two abstractions.}
112	  We show that the aggregation gap in agent observability---fixed
113	  session/span hierarchies cannot fold by semantic category---is closed
114	  by combining uniform operation records with query-time stack
115	  projections, once intent recognition restores deterministic labels
116	  (\S\ref{sec:background}--\S\ref{sec:design}).
117	\item \textbf{System: \toolname.}
118	  We implement this model as a Rust CLI with pluggable intent
119	  recognition, four built-in views, and output formats (pprof, SVG,
120	  JSON) consumable by both developers and automated analysis agents
121	  (\S\ref{sec:impl}).
122	\item \textbf{Evaluation.}
123	  We show that semantic labels separate 90\% of system-effect weight
124	  that unsemantic views merge (RQ1), that operation-stack profiling
125	  localizes hidden labeled problems with 90\% less work than flat
126	  summaries (RQ2), and that mapping-derived labels agree with
127	  ground-truth annotations on 7/9 public datasets (RQ3)
128	  (\S\ref{sec:eval}).
129	\end{enumerate}

132	\section{Background and Motivation}
133	\label{sec:background}
134	
135	\subsection{How Existing Agent Trace Models Work}
136	
137	Current agent observability tools organize traces around fixed
138	hierarchies. OpenTelemetry represents an execution as a \emph{trace}
139	containing a tree of \emph{spans}, each with a name, duration, and
140	key-value attributes. LangSmith and Langfuse group spans into
141	\emph{sessions} and display them as timelines or waterfall charts.
142	Phoenix and OpenInference add GenAI-specific span types for LLM calls,
143	tool invocations, retrieval steps, and agent reasoning.
144	
145	These models share a structural property: the session or span tree is the
146	skeleton of the data. Every event belongs to exactly one span, and spans
147	nest in a fixed parent-child hierarchy determined at execution time.
148	This design is effective for debugging: a developer can locate a failing
149	span, inspect its attributes, and trace its parent chain to understand
150	the execution context.
151	
152	\subsection{Why Fixed Hierarchies Cannot Profile}
153	
154	Profiling requires a fundamentally different operation: \emph{folding}
155	events across executions by semantic category so that width represents
156	aggregate cost. Fixed session/span hierarchies obstruct this in three
157	ways.
158	
159	\paragraph{Sessions are boundaries, not categories.}
160	A session groups events by execution, not by intent. A single session
161	may contain review, debugging, and refactoring phases; splitting by
162	session assigns all of them to the same bucket. Conversely, two sessions
163	performing the same task produce two separate buckets that cannot be
164	merged without external logic.
165	
166	\paragraph{Span names are not semantic labels.}
167	Span names describe mechanisms (\texttt{LLMCall}, \texttt{ToolInvoke},
168	\texttt{ChatCompletion}), not user intent (\texttt{review},
169	\texttt{debug}, \texttt{test}). Grouping by span name tells you how many
170	LLM calls occurred, not which categories of work consumed the budget.
171	
172	\paragraph{Concrete example.}
173	In a real development project, the system effect
174	\texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok} appears 2{,}903 times
175	across 325 sessions. A flat process summary shows a single counter; no
176	existing trace tool can disaggregate these executions by the semantic
177	intent that triggered them. We quantify this disaggregation in
178	RQ1~(\S\ref{sec:eval}).
179	
180	\subsection{Why CPU Profiling Does Not Directly Apply}
181	
182	CPU profilers solve the equivalent aggregation problem for programs.
183	A flame graph~\cite{flamegraphs} represents a profile as a set of
184	weighted \emph{samples}, each attached to a \emph{call stack} (an
185	ordered list of function frames). Identical stacks merge; width
186	represents aggregate cost. The key enabler is that function names are
187	\emph{deterministic}: the same code path always produces the same
188	frames.
189	
190	Agent traces break this precondition. As noted in \S1, prompts are
191	natural language and lack deterministic identifiers; tool calls, GUI
192	actions, and process events are named heterogeneously across agent
193	families. Raw event names cannot serve as flame-graph frames.
194	
195	These observations yield three design requirements:
196	
197	\begin{description}
198	\item[R1: Uniform record type.]
199	  Agent traces mix prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions,
200	  process events, and benchmark labels. The profiler needs a single
201	  record type that can represent all of them without type-specific
202	  objects.
203	\item[R2: Query-time aggregation.]
204	  The same data must support multiple aggregation shapes---by task,
205	  phase, action, session, or dataset---without rebuilding the trace.
206	  Sessions and spans must be fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
207	\item[R3: Deterministic labels for folding.]
208	  Free-form prompts must be mapped to short, stable, repeatable labels
209	  before folding. This \emph{intent recognition} step has no analogue in
210	  CPU profiling, where function names are already deterministic.
211	\end{description}
212	
213	%% ===================================================================
214	\section{Design}
215	\label{sec:design}
216	
217	The three requirements from \S\ref{sec:background} drive the design.
218	We introduce two abstractions---operations (\S\ref{sec:ops}) and
219	operation stacks (\S\ref{sec:stacks})---that satisfy R1 and R2, and a
220	pluggable intent-recognition mechanism (\S\ref{sec:intent}) that
221	satisfies R3.
222	
223	\subsection{Operations (R1: Uniform Record Type)}
224	\label{sec:ops}
225	
226	A profiler should not distinguish between prompts, tool calls, and
227	process events at the object-model level. \toolname uses a single
228	abstraction: an \operation is a weighted record with string fields and
229	additive measures.
230	
231	Each operation carries string fields (\texttt{project}, \texttt{agent},
232	\texttt{session}, \texttt{prompt\_tag}, \texttt{kind}, \texttt{model},
233	\texttt{path}, \texttt{domain}, \texttt{status}, \ldots) and additive
234	measures (token count, duration, occurrence count). A prompt, an LLM
235	call, a tool invocation, a file read, a GUI click, and a process event
236	are all operation records that differ only in which fields are populated.
237	This satisfies R1: the profiler does not need to distinguish event types
238	at the object-model level.
239	
240	\subsection{Operation Stacks (R2: Query-Time Aggregation)}
241	\label{sec:stacks}
242	
243	An \opstack is an ordered list of fields chosen at query time. Folding
244	operations by that list produces the standard folded-stack
245	representation:
246	
247	\begin{small}
248	\begin{verbatim}
249	CPU:   main;parse;tokenize          42
250	Agent: prompt:debug;call:llm;tool:bash  4200
251	\end{verbatim}
252	\end{small}
253	
254	\noindent Unlike CPU profiling, where the call stack is determined by
255	execution, the operation stack is determined by the query. The same
256	operations can be folded as a flat task summary, a fixed-session tree, a
257	semantic phase/action hierarchy, or a dataset-native trajectory.
258	Changing the fields changes the aggregation without changing the data.
259	
260	This directly addresses the fixed-hierarchy problem from
261	\S\ref{sec:background}: sessions and spans are optional operation fields,
262	not structural skeleton nodes. Including \texttt{session} in the stack
263	produces a per-session drilldown (equivalent to a trace tree); excluding
264	it produces a cross-session aggregate (which no existing trace tool
265	provides). The same data supports both debugging and profiling views.
266	
267	\toolname is an offline, post-hoc profiler: it reads recorded traces,
268	not live events. Runtime capture overhead belongs to AgentSight, the
269	live-capture component (\S\ref{sec:impl}).
270	
271	A \emph{view} is a triple $(\varphi, \sigma, w)$: a predicate $\varphi$
272	selects which operations participate, a stack function $\sigma$ maps each
273	operation to a frame sequence, and a weight function $w$ assigns a
274	nonnegative measure. The view formalism supports arbitrary user-defined
275	views; four built-in defaults (Table~\ref{tab:views}) answer common
276	questions:
277	
278	\begin{table}[t]
279	\centering\small
280	\caption{Built-in views. Each shares the same operation set
281	but selects different activities, stack structures, and weights.}
282	\label{tab:views}
283	\begin{tabular}{llll}
284	\toprule
285	View & $\varphi$ (select) & $w$ (width) & Question \\
286	\midrule
287	\texttt{tokens} & LLM calls & token count & Budget distribution? \\
288	\texttt{time} & All timed ops & duration (s) & Time distribution? \\
289	\texttt{files} & File-effect ops & event count & Repo coverage? \\
290	\texttt{network} & Net-effect ops & event count & External contacts? \\
291	\bottomrule
292	\end{tabular}
293	\end{table}

298	\fbox{\parbox{0.93\linewidth}{\centering\small

307	\Description{Data flow from agent traces through parsing and intent

309	\label{fig:architecture}
310	\end{figure}
311	
312	\subsection{Intent Recognition (R3: Deterministic Labels)}
313	\label{sec:intent}
314	
315	Operations and stacks handle heterogeneity and flexible aggregation, but
316	folding still requires deterministic frame labels---the precondition
317	that agent prompts violate (\S\ref{sec:background}). \toolname solves
318	this through \emph{intent recognition}: mapping free-form prompts to
319	short, stable labels before stack construction.
320	
321	The design uses a pluggable tagger framework with three backends:
322	
323	\paragraph{Regex rules with agent-assisted iteration.}
324	The production default. Rules have the form
325	\texttt{KIND:TAG=REGEX}, where \texttt{KIND} is \texttt{prompt},
326	\texttt{llm}, or \texttt{all}, \texttt{TAG} is a short lowercase label,
327	and \texttt{REGEX} is a pattern. Rules are evaluated in order; the first
328	match wins. The workflow is human--agent collaborative: run \toolname,
329	observe the unmatched rate and sample prompts, add rules, re-run, and
330	iterate until unmatched drops below 5\%. This typically takes 5--10
331	rounds. The resulting rule set is deterministic, reproducible, and
332	version-controllable.
333	
334	\paragraph{Local LLM tagger.}
335	For exploration or complex multilingual prompts, a local model
336	(e.g., a 3B-parameter GGUF via llama.cpp) generates a single-word label
337	per prompt. Grammar-constrained decoding ensures output validity.
338	Labels are cached; re-runs with unchanged prompts incur zero LLM calls.
339	
340	\paragraph{Unsupervised clustering.}
341	TF-IDF vectorization followed by K-Means discovers natural prompt groups
342	without predefined rules, feeding rule authoring.
343	
344	The one-word label design is deliberate. Flame-graph frames must be
345	short; long summaries make charts unreadable. Labels serve navigation
346	and aggregation, not correctness verdicts.
347	
348	\subsection{Mapping for Structured Traces}
349	
350	For public benchmark datasets and structured trace formats, prompts are
351	already structured: action types, tool names, environment labels, and
352	quality annotations are explicit fields. \toolname supports deterministic
353	\emph{mapping rules} that derive new operation fields from existing ones
354	before stack construction. A \emph{profile spec} records the complete
355	analysis configuration---data sources, mappings, predicates, stack
356	fields, and outputs---for deterministic replay.
357	
358	This dual path explains why \toolname handles both real agent sessions
359	(which need intent recognition) and public benchmark traces (which need
360	mapping rules): both paths produce operations with fields, and the
361	stack query works identically on both.
362	
363	%% ===================================================================
364	\section{Implementation}
365	\label{sec:impl}
366	
367	\toolname is implemented as a Rust CLI (Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}).
368	
369	\paragraph{Trace parsing.}
370	The \texttt{agent-session} crate reads Codex and Claude Code local JSONL
371	history files and reconstructs prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, and
372	their triggered file and network effects. Each prompt opens a span; LLM
373	calls, tool calls, and system effects within that span inherit its
374	semantic label. This span-based inheritance is how the profiler connects
375	semantic intent to system behavior without requiring runtime
376	instrumentation.
377	
378	\paragraph{Dataset import.}
379	Public benchmark datasets enter as operation JSONL. Mapping rules
380	(inline or via profile spec) derive fields before stack construction.
381	Standard Chrome Trace Event format can also be imported, with
382	non-\toolname protocol fields preserved as operation fields.
383	
384	\paragraph{Output formats.}
385	\toolname produces pprof protobuf (compatible with
386	\texttt{go tool pprof -http} for interactive exploration), folded-stack
387	text (compatible with Brendan Gregg's \texttt{flamegraph.pl}), standalone
388	SVG flame graphs, and JSON summaries. All outputs are deterministic given
389	the same input and profile spec.
390	
391	\paragraph{Relationship to AgentSight.}
392	\toolname is the offline profiling component of the AgentSight
393	observability framework. AgentSight provides real-time eBPF-based
394	capture of SSL traffic, process events, and file/network effects;
395	\toolname aggregates the recorded traces into semantic profiles. The two
396	tools are complementary: AgentSight answers ``what happened during this
397	run'' (debugging); \toolname answers ``where did the budget go across
398	runs'' (profiling).

401	\section{Evaluation}
402	\label{sec:eval}
403	
404	We organize the evaluation around three research questions, followed by
405	case studies and a reproducibility check.
406	
407	\paragraph{Evaluation setup.}
408	We use two classes of data. \emph{Real agent sessions}: 325 readable
409	local sessions (198~Codex, 50~Claude, 77~Claude subagent) from a
410	multi-month development project, containing 183{,}714 system
411	observations. \emph{Public labeled traces}: 15 families covering web,
412	mobile, desktop, software, API, and dialogue agents
413	(Table~\ref{tab:datasets}), totaling 47{,}590 operations through
414	mapping rules. All public traces are real agent or human executions

416	oracle-rich families (AgentRewardBench, SATraj-OS, AgentNet,
417	OSWorld-Human) provide hidden ground-truth labels for RQ2. No source
418	requires a type-specific profiler object: the same 13{,}265 operations
419	fold into 9~dataset stacks through 3{,}757~fixed-session stacks by
420	changing only the stack fields.

445	\subsection{RQ1: Does Semantic Profiling Separate What Flat Views Mix?}
446	
447	The strongest argument against semantic profiling is that traditional
448	tools ``can already see the same information.'' RQ1 tests this claim
449	directly by measuring how much system-effect weight falls into
450	\emph{mixed-intent} buckets---buckets containing observations from
451	multiple semantic regions---under different projection choices.
452	
453	\begin{table}[t]
454	\centering\small
455	\caption{Semantic-axis ablation on 183{,}714 system observations
456	from 325 real sessions. All rows preserve the same total weight.}
457	\label{tab:mixing}
458	\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
459	\toprule
460	Projection & Unique stacks & Mixed wt.\% & Residual\% \\
461	\midrule
462	No semantic labels & 11{,}967 & 90.4 & 44.7 \\
463	Session label only & 15{,}027 & 84.4 & 33.4 \\
464	Prompt label only & 24{,}703 & 36.7 & 7.5 \\
465	Session + prompt & 26{,}829 & 0.0 & 0.0 \\
466	\bottomrule
467	\end{tabular}
468	\end{table}
469	
470	Table~\ref{tab:mixing} shows the result on 325 real Codex/Claude
471	sessions. Without semantic labels, 90.4\% of system-effect weight falls
472	into mixed buckets: a flat \texttt{cargo~test} counter shows 2{,}903
473	executions but cannot distinguish whether they came from
474	\texttt{review}, \texttt{debug}, \texttt{refactor}, or \texttt{test}
475	prompts. Adding only the prompt label reduces mixed weight to 36.7\% and
476	residual to 7.5\%. The session label alone barely helps (84.4\%), because
477	sessions typically contain multiple intent phases.
478	
479	A concrete example: \texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok}
480	appears under 48 distinct prompt tags. The top tag (\texttt{refactor})
481	accounts for only 32.0\%; the remaining 68.0\% comes from
482	\texttt{review}, \texttt{research}, \texttt{test}, \texttt{explain}, and
483	others. A flat summary or process audit merges all of these.
484	
485	A label-permutation test (1{,}000 shuffles within each session) confirms
486	the separation is not random: real tags achieve 8.4\% session-beyond
487	information gain versus a null p95 of 1.9\% ($p = 0.001$). RQ3
488	evaluates the same question from a complementary angle: whether
489	mapping-derived labels agree with ground-truth annotations on public
490	datasets.
491	
492	The multi-view design is also validated by metric divergence. The
493	\texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views of the same sessions share
494	only 7/10 top prompt categories (Spearman $\rho = 0.623$).
495	\texttt{network}-tagged prompts rank 8th by time (I/O wait) but 93rd by
496	tokens. This confirms that different views answer structurally different
497	questions over the same operations.
498	
499	%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
500	\subsection{RQ2: Can Profiler Groups Localize Hidden Labeled Problems?}
501	
502	A profiler is useful if its top groups correspond to real problems: the
503	categories that concentrate failures, safety violations, or wasted
504	effort should appear at the top of the ranked output. RQ2 tests this
505	correspondence. The methodology is analogous to injecting known
506	bottlenecks in a CPU profiler evaluation: public benchmark datasets
507	provide ground-truth labels (failure, safety violation, redundant step,
508	human-task boundary); we hide these labels, run the profiler, rank the
509	resulting groups, and check whether the top groups contain the hidden
510	positives.
511	
512	\paragraph{Benchmark setup.}
513	Six tasks across four datasets: AgentRewardBench looping and
514	side-effect, SATraj-OS unsafe operation, AgentNet incorrect and redundant
515	step, and OSWorld-Human group start. Together: 34{,}539 operations,
516	3{,}699 positives. Six views (flat, fixed-session, dataset-native,
517	raw-action, operation-stack, label-drilldown) and four rankers (width,
518	visible-risk, query-aware, oracle).
519	
520	\paragraph{Localization results.}
521	
522	\begin{table*}[t]
523	\centering\small
524	\caption{RQ2 hidden-label localization (medians across six tasks).
525	Hidden policies serve only as upper bounds. WTFP = work-to-first-positive.}
526	\label{tab:localization}
527	\begin{tabular}{lrrrrrrrr}
528	\toprule
529	Policy & Hidden & AP & R@5 & F1@5 & Work@5 & R@30\% & WTFP & Groups \\
530	\midrule
531	flat:width & 0 & 0.168 & 1.000 & 0.287 & 1.000 & 0.000 & 1.000 & 1.0 \\

542	Table~\ref{tab:localization} summarizes the results. Flat summaries
543	recover all positives but require inspecting everything
544	(Work@5\,=\,1.0). Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive quickly
545	(WTFP\,=\,0.004) but fragments the workload into 285 groups with only
546	2.3\% top-five recall. Operation-stack query-aware profiling inspects
547	9.4\% of the work in the top five groups, achieves 39.0\% budget-30
548	recall, and reduces groups to 157.5.
549	
550	The result is a Pareto tradeoff, not dominance. Operation stacks improve
551	top-five recall over fixed-session drilldown on 5/6 tasks, reduce
552	median group count by 45\%, and save 90\% of inspection work versus flat
553	summaries. Fixed-session drilldown retains lower
554	work-to-first-positive on 4/6 tasks: profilers and debuggers are
555	complementary. Bootstrap (10{,}000 resamples) and label-permutation
556	(2{,}000 trials) confirm stable AP deltas exceeding the 95\%
557	prevalence/group-size null on all six tasks.
558	
559	\paragraph{Actionability: which configuration knobs explain the results?}
560	
561	Executable profile-spec patches modify stack fields, mapping rules, or
562	rankers, then re-run over the same visible operations. Five of six
563	patches improve AP, top-five lift, and first-positive work (median AP
564	delta 0.038, median top-five lift delta 0.575). Three reusable patterns
565	emerge: (1)~safety/side-effect tasks benefit from field and ranker
566	changes; (2)~step-quality tasks benefit from operation-stack
567	localization followed by fixed-session drilldown for examples;
568	(3)~human-boundary tasks require boundary-derived fields. The rejected
569	OSWorld-Human patch shows that visible rank features alone are
570	insufficient for boundary objectives; folding held-out boundary-derived
571	fields improves AP from 0.240 to 0.258 and reduces groups from 108 to
572	74, with an explicit work tradeoff.
573	
574	Rank-feature ablations identify 7 critical feature rows
575	(\texttt{repeat\_signal}, write-action, \texttt{status=success}) and 3
576	misleading rows. Guided repairs improve AP on 2/3 misleading cases but
577	use offline scored feedback, not an automatic learned ranker.
578	
579	%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
580	\subsection{RQ3: How Reliable Is Intent Recognition?}
581	
582	RQ1 and RQ2 assume that semantic labels are useful. RQ3 tests the
583	intent-recognition mechanism itself: can the tagger backends produce
584	labels that are consistent with ground-truth annotations and with each
585	other?
586	
587	\paragraph{Scale and syntax validity.}
588	On 325 real sessions, the LLM tagger processes 118{,}021 tag requests
589	(2{,}859 prompt rows, 114{,}837 LLM-call events). Of these, 82{,}886
590	hit the label cache; 35{,}136 are real llama.cpp calls to a local
591	3B-parameter model. Final tag failures: 0. On a fixed set of 300
592	redacted fragments, three model sizes (0.6B, 1.1B, 3B) all produce
593	900/900 syntactically valid outputs; p95 latencies are 23, 18, and
594	31\,ms respectively.
595	
596	\paragraph{Ground-truth agreement on public datasets.}
597	Public benchmark datasets provide native action labels that serve as
598	ground truth for mapping quality. We run a leave-dataset-out evaluation:
599	for each of 9 datasets, we train mapping rules on the other 8 and
600	measure V-measure between the mapping-derived \texttt{phase} field and
601	the dataset's native \texttt{action} labels, plus boundary F1 between
602	mapped phase boundaries and native action boundaries.
603

642	
643	\paragraph{Cross-configuration consistency.}
644	Two mapping-rule variants (differing in API/tool phase precedence) run
645	on the same 13{,}265 operations produce identical V-measure on 7/9
646	datasets; the two divergent datasets (api-bank, toolbench) differ by
647	$\leq$0.17 in V-measure. This suggests that mapping quality is robust
648	to minor rule variations on well-covered action vocabularies. Direct
649	cross-backend comparison between the regex and LLM taggers on the same
650	free-form prompts remains future work.
651	
652	\paragraph{Semantic quality versus syntactic validity.}
653	Syntactic validity does not imply semantic quality. TinyLlama 1.1B
654	achieves high exact-stability (279/300 identical across repeats) but
655	concentrates on a narrow label set, outputting
656	\texttt{localization}/\texttt{localized} disproportionately. The 3B
657	model produces a broader vocabulary (328 unique prompt tags) but includes
658	noisy entries (\texttt{agentsightsm}, \texttt{testcodex}). A
659	display-governance pipeline reduces unique tags from 1{,}546 to 1{,}364
660	through deterministic aliases, raising top-20 support coverage from
661	93.7\% to 95.2\% without overwriting raw tags. This pipeline manages
662	noise but does not establish semantic adequacy---that is what the
663	ground-truth and cross-backend checks above provide.
664	
665	%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
666	\subsection{Case Studies}
667	
668	We profile the same 325-session development project and report four
669	representative observations that illustrate the kind of aggregate
670	insights semantic flame graphs surface.
671	
672	\paragraph{Budget distribution.}
673	The \texttt{tokens} view (Figure~\ref{fig:flamegraphs}) reveals that
674	\texttt{review}-tagged prompts dominate the model budget, followed by
675	\texttt{git}, \texttt{code}, \texttt{edit}, and \texttt{debug}. A
676	timeline of 80{,}000 individual LLM calls cannot produce this
677	distribution without external aggregation. The stack further decomposes
678	each category: under \texttt{prompt:review}, the dominant sub-frames are
679	\texttt{call:llm/code} and \texttt{call:llm/tool}.
680	
681	\paragraph{Cross-session duplication.}
682	The \texttt{files} view shows \texttt{debug}-tagged prompts across
683	different sessions repeatedly accessing the same source files under
684	\texttt{collector/src/}. The flame graph aggregates these into a single
685	wide bar; a timeline shows each as an isolated event.
686	
687	\paragraph{Metric divergence.}
688	The \texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views share only 7/10 top prompt
689	categories. \texttt{network}-tagged prompts rank 8th by time (I/O wait)
690	but 93rd by tokens; \texttt{benchmark} prompts show the reverse.
691	
692	\paragraph{Path and network auditing.}
693	The \texttt{network} view attributes domain contacts to prompt

714	\subsection{Reproducibility}
715	
716	All results are backed by profile specs for deterministic replay. We
717	re-execute 76 tracked specs twice (152 invocations); all produce

722	%% ===================================================================
723	\section{Related Work}
724	
725	\textbf{Profiling and flame graphs.}
726	Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and pprof~\cite{pprof} establish the
727	folded-stack lineage: profiles are weighted samples with location
728	hierarchies. Pprof supports sample labels and can visualize them as
729	pseudo stack frames through tag-root/tag-leaf options. Perfetto
730	generalizes trace ingestion with SQL-based analysis and derived
731	events~\cite{perfetto}. These systems support query-time aggregation, so
732	\toolname does not claim novelty for flexible aggregation alone. The
733	difference is the domain: samples are agent operations, frames are
734	semantic labels derived from natural-language prompts through intent
735	recognition, and the evaluation scores profiler output against hidden
736	agent-trajectory labels.
737	
738	\textbf{Agent tracing and LLM observability.}
739	OpenTelemetry GenAI and OpenInference standardize GenAI
740	spans~\cite{otel, openinference}. LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
741	Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, and Phoenix~\cite{phoenix} provide trace
742	visualization, session management, evaluations, and dashboards.
743	AgentOps~\cite{agentops} argues for structured agent observability
744	covering goals, plans, tools, and artifacts. These systems excel at
745	single-execution debugging: timeline views, span trees, and waterfall
746	charts help locate a specific failure. \toolname complements them with
747	cross-session aggregate profiling.
748	Datadog LLM Observability adds topic clustering over user messages, and
749	Laminar Signals extracts structured events from traces. These are steps
750	toward semantic aggregation, but they characterize \emph{input
751	distributions} (``30\% of users ask code questions''), not
752	\emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks consume 40\% of the
753	token budget''). \toolname produces the latter through folded-stack
754	aggregation where width represents cost.
755	
756	\textbf{Agent failure diagnosis.}
757	AgentRx~\cite{agentrx} releases annotated failure trajectories and uses
758	constraint checking plus an LLM judge for root-cause localization.
759	TELBench~\cite{telbench} builds span-localization benchmarks from
760	semantic error annotations. AgentAtlas argues that outcome leaderboards
761	miss trajectory-level quality. These systems perform \emph{span-level}
762	fault localization within a single execution: which step failed and why.
763	\toolname performs \emph{category-level} aggregate profiling: which
764	categories of work produce the most failures, consume the most budget,
765	or generate repeated system effects across sessions.
766	
767	%% ===================================================================
768	\section{Discussion}
769	
770	\paragraph{Profiler and debugger are complementary.}
771	Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive faster on 4/6 tasks
772	(RQ2). This is expected: debuggers are designed for single-case
773	investigation. The profiler identifies \emph{which categories} deserve
774	attention; the debugger explains \emph{what happened} in a specific
775	case. \toolname supports both by including or excluding session fields in
776	the stack query. A typical workflow starts with the profiler (``review
777	tasks dominate the budget''), then drills into individual sessions to
778	understand why.
779	
780	\paragraph{Agent-as-consumer.}
781	The profiler's structured output (JSON, pprof, folded stacks) is
782	designed to be consumed by automated analysis agents, not only human
783	developers. The RQ2 ranker strategies demonstrate this pattern: a
784	scoring policy reads profiler output, ranks groups by visible features,
785	and identifies high-cost or high-failure categories. In practice, an AI
786	coding agent can run \texttt{agentpprof --format json}, parse the output,
787	and recommend configuration changes---the same workflow that the
788	regex-rule iteration (\S\ref{sec:design}) already uses. This positions
789	semantic profiling as infrastructure for agent self-diagnosis, not only
790	for human inspection.
791	
792	\paragraph{Limitations.}
793	The real-session data (RQ1, RQ3, case studies) comes from one developer
794	on one project. RQ2 mitigates this with four independent public datasets
795	containing real agent traces from different research groups, but
796	multi-project and multi-user real-session evaluation would strengthen the
797	generality claim. The evaluation measures label-scored profiler fidelity,
798	not human or agent productivity. A controlled study comparing
799	flame-graph-guided diagnosis against timeline-based diagnosis would test
800	the practical value but is not required for the profiler-mechanism
801	contribution. \toolname currently reads Codex/Claude local histories and
802	operation JSONL; OpenTelemetry, LangSmith, and Langfuse trace imports are
803	engineering work, not design obstacles.
804	
805	%% ===================================================================
806	\section{Conclusion}
807	
808	Agent observability needs profiling, not only debugging. The obstacle is
809	that natural-language prompts lack the deterministic identifiers that
810	make flame-graph folding work. \toolname shows that two
811	abstractions---operations and operation stacks---close this gap once
812	intent recognition restores deterministic labels. The evaluation
813	confirms that semantic profiling separates information flat views merge,
814	localizes labeled problems with less work than both flat summaries and
815	fixed-session drilldown, and produces labels that agree with
816	ground-truth annotations across heterogeneous public datasets.
817	
818	The main limitation is single-project real-session data; multi-project
819	evaluation and direct cross-backend tagger comparison are next steps.
820	The most impactful direction is trace-ecosystem integration:
821	importing OpenTelemetry and LangSmith traces as operations would let
822	\toolname profile any instrumented agent without a custom parser.

\begin{document}

\title{AgentPProf: Semantic Profiling for AI Agent Traces}

\begin{abstract}
% Beat 1: Context
AI agents produce complex execution traces spanning prompts, LLM calls,
tool invocations, GUI actions, and system effects. As deployments grow
to hundreds of sessions, both human operators and automated analysis
pipelines need aggregate views---not just per-execution debugging.

% Beat 2: Problem
Existing observability tools organize events into fixed session/span
hierarchies suited for single-run debugging but unable to fold events
across sessions by semantic work category. CPU flame graphs solve the
equivalent aggregation problem for programs, but they rely on
deterministic function names; agent prompts are natural language and
cannot be folded directly.

% Beat 3: This paper
We show that agent profiling reduces to two abstractions once intent
recognition restores the deterministic-label precondition. An
\emph{operation} is a uniform weighted record for any agent activity; an
\emph{operation stack} is a field projection chosen at query time.
Sessions and spans become optional fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
\toolname implements this model with pluggable intent-recognition
backends (regex rules, local LLM tagging, unsupervised clustering) and
produces flame graphs, pprof profiles, and structured JSON consumable by
both developers and analysis agents.

% Beat 4: Results
On 325 real agent sessions, semantic labels separate 90\% of
system-effect weight that flat views merge. On four public datasets
(34{,}539 operations), operation-stack profiling reduces inspection work
by 90\% versus flat summaries and fragmentation by 45\% versus
fixed-session drilldown. Leave-dataset-out mapping achieves V-measure
above 0.7 on 7/9 held-out datasets.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

%% ===================================================================
\section{Introduction}

AI agent systems produce execution traces that interleave prompts, LLM
calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, process events, and benchmark
labels. As agent deployments scale to hundreds of sessions and tens of
thousands of calls, both developers and automated analysis agents need
to answer aggregate questions: which categories of work consume the most
tokens, where do repeated failures concentrate, and how does cost
distribute across semantic task families? Existing observability
tools---LangSmith~\cite{langsmith}, Langfuse~\cite{langfuse},
Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, OpenTelemetry GenAI~\cite{otel}---organize
events into per-execution timelines and span trees, enabling
single-run debugging. But no existing tool provides an aggregate view
that folds heterogeneous events across sessions into a cost or frequency
distribution grouped by semantic work category.

CPU profilers solved the equivalent problem for programs: flame
graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} fold millions of function-call samples into
a single chart where width represents cost. The key enabler is
\emph{deterministic} function names that merge identical call stacks.
Agent traces break this assumption---prompts are natural language, and
two prompts expressing the same intent share no characters. We develop
this gap and the design requirements it implies in
\S\ref{sec:background}.

The central insight is that agent observability requires
\emph{profiling}---aggregate, semantic, cross-session cost
attribution---not only per-execution debugging, and that the obstacle to
applying classical profiler techniques is the nondeterminism of
natural-language identifiers. This paper presents \toolname, a profiler
that restores aggregate flame-graph analysis for agent traces. The
profiler is built on two abstractions: an \emph{operation} (a uniform
weighted record for any agent activity) and an \emph{operation stack}
(a field projection chosen at query time). Sessions, spans, and trace
identifiers are operation fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
\emph{Intent recognition}---mapping free-form prompts to stable labels
through pluggable backends (regex rules, local LLM tagging, or
unsupervised clustering)---restores the deterministic-label precondition
that flame-graph folding requires.

Some existing tools take steps toward semantic grouping: Datadog LLM
Observability clusters user messages by topic, and Laminar extracts
structured signals from traces. These characterize \emph{input
distributions} (``30\% of users ask code questions'') but not
\emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks consume 40\% of the
token budget''). \toolname produces the latter through folded-stack
aggregation where width represents cost.

This paper makes three contributions:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Insight: agent profiling reduces to two abstractions.}
  We show that the aggregation gap in agent observability---fixed
  session/span hierarchies cannot fold by semantic category---is closed
  by combining uniform operation records with query-time stack
  projections, once intent recognition restores deterministic labels
  (\S\ref{sec:background}--\S\ref{sec:design}).
\item \textbf{System: \toolname.}
  We implement this model as a Rust CLI with pluggable intent
  recognition, four built-in views, and output formats (pprof, SVG,
  JSON) consumable by both developers and automated analysis agents
  (\S\ref{sec:impl}).
\item \textbf{Evaluation.}
  We show that semantic labels separate 90\% of system-effect weight
  that unsemantic views merge (RQ1), that operation-stack profiling
  localizes hidden labeled problems with 90\% less work than flat
  summaries (RQ2), and that mapping-derived labels agree with
  ground-truth annotations on 7/9 public datasets (RQ3)
  (\S\ref{sec:eval}).
\end{enumerate}

%% ===================================================================
\section{Background and Motivation}
\label{sec:background}

\subsection{How Existing Agent Trace Models Work}

Current agent observability tools organize traces around fixed
hierarchies. OpenTelemetry represents an execution as a \emph{trace}
containing a tree of \emph{spans}, each with a name, duration, and
key-value attributes. LangSmith and Langfuse group spans into
\emph{sessions} and display them as timelines or waterfall charts.
Phoenix and OpenInference add GenAI-specific span types for LLM calls,
tool invocations, retrieval steps, and agent reasoning.

These models share a structural property: the session or span tree is the
skeleton of the data. Every event belongs to exactly one span, and spans
nest in a fixed parent-child hierarchy determined at execution time.
This design is effective for debugging: a developer can locate a failing
span, inspect its attributes, and trace its parent chain to understand
the execution context.

\subsection{Why Fixed Hierarchies Cannot Profile}

Profiling requires a fundamentally different operation: \emph{folding}
events across executions by semantic category so that width represents
aggregate cost. Fixed session/span hierarchies obstruct this in three
ways.

\paragraph{Sessions are boundaries, not categories.}
A session groups events by execution, not by intent. A single session
may contain review, debugging, and refactoring phases; splitting by
session assigns all of them to the same bucket. Conversely, two sessions
performing the same task produce two separate buckets that cannot be
merged without external logic.

\paragraph{Span names are not semantic labels.}
Span names describe mechanisms (\texttt{LLMCall}, \texttt{ToolInvoke},
\texttt{ChatCompletion}), not user intent (\texttt{review},
\texttt{debug}, \texttt{test}). Grouping by span name tells you how many
LLM calls occurred, not which categories of work consumed the budget.

\paragraph{Concrete example.}
In a real development project, the system effect
\texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok} appears 2{,}903 times
across 325 sessions. A flat process summary shows a single counter; no
existing trace tool can disaggregate these executions by the semantic
intent that triggered them. We quantify this disaggregation in
RQ1~(\S\ref{sec:eval}).

\subsection{Why CPU Profiling Does Not Directly Apply}

CPU profilers solve the equivalent aggregation problem for programs.
A flame graph~\cite{flamegraphs} represents a profile as a set of
weighted \emph{samples}, each attached to a \emph{call stack} (an
ordered list of function frames). Identical stacks merge; width
represents aggregate cost. The key enabler is that function names are
\emph{deterministic}: the same code path always produces the same
frames.

Agent traces break this precondition. As noted in \S1, prompts are
natural language and lack deterministic identifiers; tool calls, GUI
actions, and process events are named heterogeneously across agent
families. Raw event names cannot serve as flame-graph frames.

These observations yield three design requirements:

\begin{description}
\item[R1: Uniform record type.]
  Agent traces mix prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions,
  process events, and benchmark labels. The profiler needs a single
  record type that can represent all of them without type-specific
  objects.
\item[R2: Query-time aggregation.]
  The same data must support multiple aggregation shapes---by task,
  phase, action, session, or dataset---without rebuilding the trace.
  Sessions and spans must be fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
\item[R3: Deterministic labels for folding.]
  Free-form prompts must be mapped to short, stable, repeatable labels
  before folding. This \emph{intent recognition} step has no analogue in
  CPU profiling, where function names are already deterministic.
\end{description}

\section{Design}
\label{sec:design}

The three requirements from \S\ref{sec:background} drive the design.
We introduce two abstractions---operations (\S\ref{sec:ops}) and
operation stacks (\S\ref{sec:stacks})---that satisfy R1 and R2, and a
pluggable intent-recognition mechanism (\S\ref{sec:intent}) that
satisfies R3.

\subsection{Operations (R1: Uniform Record Type)}
\label{sec:ops}

A profiler should not distinguish between prompts, tool calls, and
process events at the object-model level. \toolname uses a single
abstraction: an \operation is a weighted record with string fields and
additive measures.

Each operation carries string fields (\texttt{project}, \texttt{agent},
\texttt{session}, \texttt{prompt\_tag}, \texttt{kind}, \texttt{model},
\texttt{path}, \texttt{domain}, \texttt{status}, \ldots) and additive
measures (token count, duration, occurrence count). A prompt, an LLM
call, a tool invocation, a file read, a GUI click, and a process event
are all operation records that differ only in which fields are populated.
This satisfies R1: the profiler does not need to distinguish event types
at the object-model level.

\subsection{Operation Stacks (R2: Query-Time Aggregation)}
\label{sec:stacks}

An \opstack is an ordered list of fields chosen at query time. Folding
operations by that list produces the standard folded-stack
representation:

\begin{small}
\begin{verbatim}
CPU:   main;parse;tokenize          42
Agent: prompt:debug;call:llm;tool:bash  4200
\end{verbatim}
\end{small}

\noindent Unlike CPU profiling, where the call stack is determined by
execution, the operation stack is determined by the query. The same
operations can be folded as a flat task summary, a fixed-session tree, a
semantic phase/action hierarchy, or a dataset-native trajectory.
Changing the fields changes the aggregation without changing the data.

This directly addresses the fixed-hierarchy problem from
\S\ref{sec:background}: sessions and spans are optional operation fields,
not structural skeleton nodes. Including \texttt{session} in the stack
produces a per-session drilldown (equivalent to a trace tree); excluding
it produces a cross-session aggregate (which no existing trace tool
provides). The same data supports both debugging and profiling views.

\toolname is an offline, post-hoc profiler: it reads recorded traces,
not live events. Runtime capture overhead belongs to AgentSight, the
live-capture component (\S\ref{sec:impl}).

A \emph{view} is a triple $(\varphi, \sigma, w)$: a predicate $\varphi$
selects which operations participate, a stack function $\sigma$ maps each
operation to a frame sequence, and a weight function $w$ assigns a
nonnegative measure. The view formalism supports arbitrary user-defined
views; four built-in defaults (Table~\ref{tab:views}) answer common
questions:

\subsection{Intent Recognition (R3: Deterministic Labels)}
\label{sec:intent}

Operations and stacks handle heterogeneity and flexible aggregation, but
folding still requires deterministic frame labels---the precondition
that agent prompts violate (\S\ref{sec:background}). \toolname solves
this through \emph{intent recognition}: mapping free-form prompts to
short, stable labels before stack construction.

The design uses a pluggable tagger framework with three backends:

\paragraph{Regex rules with agent-assisted iteration.}
The production default. Rules have the form
\texttt{KIND:TAG=REGEX}, where \texttt{KIND} is \texttt{prompt},
\texttt{llm}, or \texttt{all}, \texttt{TAG} is a short lowercase label,
and \texttt{REGEX} is a pattern. Rules are evaluated in order; the first
match wins. The workflow is human--agent collaborative: run \toolname,
observe the unmatched rate and sample prompts, add rules, re-run, and
iterate until unmatched drops below 5\%. This typically takes 5--10
rounds. The resulting rule set is deterministic, reproducible, and
version-controllable.

\paragraph{Local LLM tagger.}
For exploration or complex multilingual prompts, a local model
(e.g., a 3B-parameter GGUF via llama.cpp) generates a single-word label
per prompt. Grammar-constrained decoding ensures output validity.
Labels are cached; re-runs with unchanged prompts incur zero LLM calls.

\paragraph{Unsupervised clustering.}
TF-IDF vectorization followed by K-Means discovers natural prompt groups
without predefined rules, feeding rule authoring.

The one-word label design is deliberate. Flame-graph frames must be
short; long summaries make charts unreadable. Labels serve navigation
and aggregation, not correctness verdicts.

\subsection{Mapping for Structured Traces}

For public benchmark datasets and structured trace formats, prompts are
already structured: action types, tool names, environment labels, and
quality annotations are explicit fields. \toolname supports deterministic
\emph{mapping rules} that derive new operation fields from existing ones
before stack construction. A \emph{profile spec} records the complete
analysis configuration---data sources, mappings, predicates, stack
fields, and outputs---for deterministic replay.

This dual path explains why \toolname handles both real agent sessions
(which need intent recognition) and public benchmark traces (which need
mapping rules): both paths produce operations with fields, and the
stack query works identically on both.

\section{Implementation}
\label{sec:impl}

\toolname is implemented as a Rust CLI (Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}).

\paragraph{Trace parsing.}
The \texttt{agent-session} crate reads Codex and Claude Code local JSONL
history files and reconstructs prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, and
their triggered file and network effects. Each prompt opens a span; LLM
calls, tool calls, and system effects within that span inherit its
semantic label. This span-based inheritance is how the profiler connects
semantic intent to system behavior without requiring runtime
instrumentation.

\paragraph{Dataset import.}
Public benchmark datasets enter as operation JSONL. Mapping rules
(inline or via profile spec) derive fields before stack construction.
Standard Chrome Trace Event format can also be imported, with
non-\toolname protocol fields preserved as operation fields.

\paragraph{Output formats.}
\toolname produces pprof protobuf (compatible with
\texttt{go tool pprof -http} for interactive exploration), folded-stack
text (compatible with Brendan Gregg's \texttt{flamegraph.pl}), standalone
SVG flame graphs, and JSON summaries. All outputs are deterministic given
the same input and profile spec.

\paragraph{Relationship to AgentSight.}
\toolname is the offline profiling component of the AgentSight
observability framework. AgentSight provides real-time eBPF-based
capture of SSL traffic, process events, and file/network effects;
\toolname aggregates the recorded traces into semantic profiles. The two
tools are complementary: AgentSight answers ``what happened during this
run'' (debugging); \toolname answers ``where did the budget go across
runs'' (profiling).

\subsection{RQ1: Does Semantic Profiling Separate What Flat Views Mix?}

The strongest argument against semantic profiling is that traditional

multiple semantic regions---under different projection choices.

\subsection{RQ2: Can Profiler Groups Localize Hidden Labeled Problems?}

\subsection{RQ3: How Reliable Is Intent Recognition?}

RQ1 and RQ2 assume that semantic labels are useful. RQ3 tests the
intent-recognition mechanism itself: can the tagger backends produce
labels that are consistent with ground-truth annotations and with each
other?

\paragraph{Scale and syntax validity.}
On 325 real sessions, the LLM tagger processes 118{,}021 tag requests
(2{,}859 prompt rows, 114{,}837 LLM-call events). Of these, 82{,}886
hit the label cache; 35{,}136 are real llama.cpp calls to a local

redacted fragments, three model sizes (0.6B, 1.1B, 3B) all produce

31\,ms respectively.

through deterministic aliases, raising top-20 support coverage from
93.7\% to 95.2\% without overwriting raw tags. This pipeline manages
noise but does not establish semantic adequacy---that is what the
ground-truth and cross-backend checks above provide.

\section{Related Work}

\textbf{Profiling and flame graphs.}
Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and pprof~\cite{pprof} establish the
folded-stack lineage: profiles are weighted samples with location
hierarchies. Pprof supports sample labels and can visualize them as
pseudo stack frames through tag-root/tag-leaf options. Perfetto
generalizes trace ingestion with SQL-based analysis and derived
events~\cite{perfetto}. These systems support query-time aggregation, so
\toolname does not claim novelty for flexible aggregation alone. The
difference is the domain: samples are agent operations, frames are
semantic labels derived from natural-language prompts through intent
recognition, and the evaluation scores profiler output against hidden
agent-trajectory labels.

\textbf{Agent tracing and LLM observability.}
OpenTelemetry GenAI and OpenInference standardize GenAI
spans~\cite{otel, openinference}. LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, and Phoenix~\cite{phoenix} provide trace
visualization, session management, evaluations, and dashboards.
AgentOps~\cite{agentops} argues for structured agent observability
covering goals, plans, tools, and artifacts. These systems excel at
single-execution debugging: timeline views, span trees, and waterfall
charts help locate a specific failure. \toolname complements them with
cross-session aggregate profiling.
Datadog LLM Observability adds topic clustering over user messages, and
Laminar Signals extracts structured events from traces. These are steps
toward semantic aggregation, but they characterize \emph{input
distributions} (``30\% of users ask code questions''), not
\emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks consume 40\% of the
token budget''). \toolname produces the latter through folded-stack
aggregation where width represents cost.

\textbf{Agent failure diagnosis.}
AgentRx~\cite{agentrx} releases annotated failure trajectories and uses
constraint checking plus an LLM judge for root-cause localization.
TELBench~\cite{telbench} builds span-localization benchmarks from
semantic error annotations. AgentAtlas argues that outcome leaderboards
miss trajectory-level quality. These systems perform \emph{span-level}
fault localization within a single execution: which step failed and why.
\toolname performs \emph{category-level} aggregate profiling: which
categories of work produce the most failures, consume the most budget,
or generate repeated system effects across sessions.

\section{Discussion}

\paragraph{Profiler and debugger are complementary.}
Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive faster on 4/6 tasks
(RQ2). This is expected: debuggers are designed for single-case
investigation. The profiler identifies \emph{which categories} deserve
attention; the debugger explains \emph{what happened} in a specific
case. \toolname supports both by including or excluding session fields in
the stack query. A typical workflow starts with the profiler (``review
tasks dominate the budget''), then drills into individual sessions to
understand why.

\paragraph{Agent-as-consumer.}
The profiler's structured output (JSON, pprof, folded stacks) is
designed to be consumed by automated analysis agents, not only human
developers. The RQ2 ranker strategies demonstrate this pattern: a
scoring policy reads profiler output, ranks groups by visible features,
and identifies high-cost or high-failure categories. In practice, an AI
coding agent can run \texttt{agentpprof --format json}, parse the output,
and recommend configuration changes---the same workflow that the
regex-rule iteration (\S\ref{sec:design}) already uses. This positions
semantic profiling as infrastructure for agent self-diagnosis, not only
for human inspection.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
The real-session data (RQ1, RQ3, case studies) comes from one developer
on one project. RQ2 mitigates this with four independent public datasets
containing real agent traces from different research groups, but
multi-project and multi-user real-session evaluation would strengthen the
generality claim. The evaluation measures label-scored profiler fidelity,
not human or agent productivity. A controlled study comparing
flame-graph-guided diagnosis against timeline-based diagnosis would test
the practical value but is not required for the profiler-mechanism
contribution. \toolname currently reads Codex/Claude local histories and
operation JSONL; OpenTelemetry, LangSmith, and Langfuse trace imports are
engineering work, not design obstacles.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Conclusion}

Agent observability needs profiling, not only debugging. The obstacle is
that natural-language prompts lack the deterministic identifiers that
make flame-graph folding work. \toolname shows that two
abstractions---operations and operation stacks---close this gap once
intent recognition restores deterministic labels. The evaluation
confirms that semantic profiling separates information flat views merge,
localizes labeled problems with less work than both flat summaries and
fixed-session drilldown, and produces labels that agree with
ground-truth annotations across heterogeneous public datasets.

The main limitation is single-project real-session data; multi-project
evaluation and direct cross-backend tagger comparison are next steps.
The most impactful direction is trace-ecosystem integration:
importing OpenTelemetry and LangSmith traces as operations would let
\toolname profile any instrumented agent without a custom parser.

Now let me work through the six review dimensions systematically.

---

## Phase 1 — Logic and Claims Review

### 1. Thesis Clarity

The thesis is stated at line 85–88: "agent observability requires profiling—aggregate, semantic, cross-session cost attribution—not only per-execution debugging, and the obstacle is the nondeterminism of natural-language identifiers." It is also restated in the abstract (line 38) and the conclusion (line 808). The thesis is clear and consistently present.

However, the thesis has two parts—(a) "profiling is needed" and (b) "nondeterminism is the obstacle"—and only (b) has a technical solution. Part (a) is an observation, not a contribution. The paper could strengthen this by treating (a) as context and foregrounding (b)+solution as the thesis.

### 2. Claim–Evidence Alignment

| Contribution claim | Evidence | Gap? |
|---|---|---|
| C1: "agent profiling reduces to two abstractions" | §2 motivates requirements; §3 defines operations + stacks; Eval setup shows 15 datasets fold without type-specific objects | The "reduces to" claim is argued by design but **never tested negatively**: no experiment shows that adding a third object type (e.g., a session object) would be worse. The generality numbers (9→3757 stacks) are presented in the eval setup paragraph, not a dedicated subsection—easy to miss. |
| C2: "System: AgentPProf" | §4 Implementation | Adequate for a system contribution. |
| C3: "RQ1 separation / RQ2 localization / RQ3 label quality" | Tables 3, 4, 5 | See per-RQ analysis below. |

### 3. Motivation Completeness

R1/R2/R3 are well-motivated. A reviewer could argue R1 is trivially satisfied by any key-value record format (JSON), but the paper partially addresses this by noting the profiler *doesn't distinguish* types at the object-model level. R2 is the genuinely novel requirement. R3 is well-motivated by the CPU analogy.

One gap: R1–R3 do not mention **weight semantics**. The view formalism $(\varphi, \sigma, w)$ introduces $w$ (weight function) as a new concept in §3.2, but no requirement demands it. Adding "R1b: the record must carry additive measures so that width represents cost" would make the view formalism feel motivated rather than introduced ad hoc.

### 4. Evaluation Coverage

**RQ1** tests separation, not the two-abstraction model. The mixing metric shows labels add value, but it does not test whether *operation stacks* add value over, say, a simple GROUP BY on the prompt_tag field. A SQL query `SELECT prompt_tag, COUNT(*) FROM events GROUP BY prompt_tag` would also separate cargo-test by intent. What operations+stacks add is *recursive depth*—the ability to fold at task/phase/action/session levels. This is mentioned in the eval setup (9→3757 stacks) but not tested as an RQ1 result.

**RQ2** tests localization, which the paper now correctly frames as "a profiler is useful if its top groups correspond to real problems." The Pareto claim is honest: counterpoints (fixed-session WTFP wins on 4/6) are stated. The actionability sub-section strengthens this with concrete patch results.

**RQ3** tests mapping quality via V-measure, not intent-recognition quality. The LLM tagger's scale/latency numbers (lines 587–594) are engineering metrics, not quality evidence. The V-measure table tests *mapping rules* on structured datasets, not *intent recognition* on free-form prompts. The paper should be explicit that RQ3 evaluates the mapping path (for structured traces) but not the intent-recognition path (for free-form prompts) at the quality level—only at the syntax/scale level.

### 5. Logical Gaps

- §2.2 "Concrete example" (line 172–178) forward-references RQ1, but in RQ1 the same example is used as evidence. This is circular: the motivation cites the result, and the result cites the motivation.
- The "agent-as-consumer" discussion (line 780–790) claims profiler output is designed for automated agents, but no evaluation tests this. The RQ2 ranker strategies are described as a "prototype of this pattern," but they are not evaluated *as* agent consumption—they are evaluated as ranking algorithms.
- The 15-dataset generality evidence (lines 417–420) is buried in the eval setup paragraph. If "the two abstractions suffice for heterogeneous traces" is contribution C1, this evidence deserves more prominence.

### 6. Strongest Reviewer Attacks

**Attack 1: "Operations are JSON records; operation stacks are GROUP BY. This is data engineering, not research."**
Current defense: the paper argues the *combination* with intent recognition and the hidden-label evaluation methodology is novel. The defense is scattered; it should be consolidated in §1 or §6 Related Work. The strongest counter is that pprof also "just" does GROUP BY on call stacks—the contribution is identifying the right GROUP BY dimensions for agent traces and evaluating them.

**Attack 2: "RQ1 and RQ3 test labels, not the two-abstraction model. Where is the evidence that operation stacks matter?"**
Current defense: the eval setup mentions 9→3757 stacks, and RQ2's multiple-view comparison includes operation-stack vs flat/fixed-session/raw-action. But RQ1 doesn't isolate stacks from labels. A dedicated comparison—same labels, different stack depths—would close this. The depth-aware scoring data from V2 (20/24 task-depth rows) exists in the artifact set but is not in the paper.

**Attack 3: "All real-session data comes from one developer on one project. The labels might just reflect this user's vocabulary."**
Current defense: Limitations paragraph (line 792–803). This is acknowledged but not mitigated. The permutation test (p=0.001) helps but tests statistical non-randomness, not generalizability.

---

## Findings

### Must-fix

**M1 — RQ1 does not test the stack abstraction, only the labels.** (§5.1, lines 445–497)
RQ1's mixing metric shows labels separate intent. It does not show that query-time stack selection (R2) adds value over a simple label-based GROUP BY. The paper's headline contribution is "two abstractions," but only one (intent labels via R3) is tested in RQ1.
**Fix:** Add a paragraph to RQ1 showing the recursive stack-depth result: the same 13,265 operations fold from 9 dataset stacks to 3,757 fixed-session stacks. Alternatively, show that at different stack depths the profiler answers different questions (e.g., task-level vs action-level vs session-level views produce different top-cost categories). This data exists in the eval setup paragraph—promote it to an RQ1 result.

**M2 — RQ3 conflates mapping quality (on structured traces) with intent-recognition quality (on free-form prompts).** (§5.3, lines 580–663)
The V-measure table evaluates mapping rules, not the LLM/regex tagger. The LLM tagger section reports only scale/syntax. The paper's contribution C1 names intent recognition as a key mechanism, but its quality on free-form prompts is never evaluated against ground truth.
**Fix:** Either (a) add a sentence explicitly scoping RQ3: "RQ3 evaluates the mapping path for structured traces; the intent-recognition path for free-form prompts is evaluated only at the syntax/scale level, with quality assessment left as future work"; or (b) design a small experiment on a structured dataset where you *also* run the LLM tagger on the action-description text field and compare its labels to the ground-truth action type.

**M3 — The "reduces to two abstractions" claim (C1) lacks negative evidence.** (§1 line 111)
The paper argues operations+stacks are sufficient. It never argues they are *necessary* or that alternatives (e.g., a session+label model, a span-tree+label model) would be worse.
**Fix:** In RQ2, the comparison already includes fixed-session views (which are a session+label model) and dataset-native views (which are span-tree-shaped). Explicitly note that these are alternative abstractions that the two-abstraction model subsumes. The fact that operation stacks beat fixed-session on 5/6 recall metrics is evidence that the stack abstraction adds value over a fixed session model. Currently this comparison is framed as "baselines"; reframe it as "testing whether the two-abstraction model outperforms fixed-hierarchy alternatives."

### Should-fix

**S1 — The 15-dataset generality evidence is buried in the eval setup paragraph.** (Lines 407–420)
If C1 claims "two abstractions suffice for heterogeneous traces," the evidence (15 families, 47,590 ops, no type-specific objects) should be a visible result, not a setup detail.
**Fix:** Either (a) give it a short dedicated paragraph with a clear result statement after the setup, or (b) add one sentence to RQ1: "The same two-abstraction model covers all 15 trace families (Table 2) without type-specific objects."

**S2 — RQ1's information gain (8.4% vs null p95 1.9%) is statistically significant but practically small.** (Line 486)
A reviewer may note that 8.4% information gain is a modest effect size. The paper should contextualize: the useful outcome is not the raw information-gain number but the 90.4%→36.7% mixing reduction, which is large. The permutation test is a *significance check*, not the *primary metric*.
**Fix:** Reorder the RQ1 discussion: lead with the mixing table (primary evidence), then use the permutation test as a robustness check rather than a standalone result.

**S3 — The Datadog/Laminar paragraph in §1 (lines 100–106) lacks citations.** (Lines 100–106)
**Fix:** Add product-documentation URLs or footnotes.

### Consider

**C1 — The abstract may exceed ACM sigconf's 150-word limit.** At ~200 words it is borderline. Check the venue's requirements.

**C2 — The case studies (§5.5) are disconnected from any RQ.** They illustrate profiling utility but are not linked to C1, C2, or C3. One sentence linking them to the "profiling vs debugging" thesis would help: "These observations demonstrate the aggregate, cross-session insights that motivate the profiling abstraction (C1)."

**C3 — The paper never defines what "semantic" means in "semantic profiling."** The word appears in the title and throughout but is used loosely. It sometimes means "intent-labeled" and sometimes means "not-session-level." A one-sentence definition ("by *semantic* we mean labeled by user intent rather than by execution structure") would prevent a reviewer from objecting to the vagueness.
